articles.title: Urgent appeal to find woman after suspected human tissue discovered in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Police fear a woman who may have recently given birth needs urgent medical attention after a discovery near Watkins Street and Charter Street, off Kingsway.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS | ONGOING AND DEVELOPING STORY. This report will be updated when further verified information becomes available.

Detectives are trying to find a woman who may need urgent medical attention after suspected human tissue was discovered off Kingsway in Rochdale.

Greater Manchester Police said evidence found near the junction of Watkins Street and Charter Street suggests a woman may have recently given birth. Officers were called shortly before 9am on Thursday 22 October.

Police have been examining the scene and carrying out enquiries. Their priority is to find the woman and make sure she is safe and well.

Detective Inspector Daniel Daly, from GMP's Rochdale CID, said: “She may be in need of urgent medical attention, and she is our absolute priority at the moment - that is why we are asking anyone with information to contact us.”

Anyone with information, or who may have seen a woman in distress, should call 101 and quote incident number 684 of 22/10/2026.

Information can also be reported online or through GMP's LiveChat service at https://www.gmp.police.uk. Alternatively, contact Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

DI Daly asked the public not to speculate: “We would ask that people don't speculate on the circumstances of this discovery as it hinders our investigation and is upsetting for those involved.”

The information in this report comes from Greater Manchester Police's appeal issued on 22 October 2026. Police have not confirmed further circumstances in that appeal.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: Short answer: no—there’s no evidence for supernatural visitors, but the place-name, a nineteenth‑century literary tradition and a distinctive rock ‘chapel’ have combined to make Healey Dell one of Rochdale’s best-loved bits of local folklore.
articles.summary: Short answer: no—there’s no evidence for supernatural visitors, but the place-name, a nineteenth‑century literary tradition and a distinctive rock ‘chapel’ have combined to make Healey Dell one of Rochdale’s best-loved bits of local folklore.
articles.body:
Ask a local where the Fairies’ Chapel is and they’ll point you down the steps from Station Road, into the ravine by the River Spodden. Ask whether fairies live there and the practical answer is simple: no verifiable evidence supports the existence of fairies; what the records do show is a named rock formation, a cluster of old stories collected in the nineteenth century and a long history of people visiting the site because the place feels, to many, a little uncanny. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

Those are not trivial facts. Healey Dell is a designated Local Nature Reserve and an area of industrial archaeology that straddles borough boundaries; part of the valley was legally made a statutory LNR in April 1976. The most dramatic built feature is the Healey Dell Viaduct, a high, eight‑arched sandstone railway viaduct that is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. Those designations are documentary and can be checked. ([rossendale.gov.uk](https://www.rossendale.gov.uk/download/meetings/id/4148/e2_appendix_2))

The Dell’s historical record is everyday, material and useful. The valley contains the remains of nineteenth‑century mills and the disused Rochdale‑to‑Bacup railway line; archaeological and conservation surveys catalogue those features and guide how the reserve is managed for wildlife and visitors. Management is led locally by Rochdale (and neighbouring Rossendale) authorities and by volunteer groups; published ecological reports and neighbourhood plans reference Healey Dell when mapping green infrastructure for the area. That is the part of the story that affects readers’ lives—path repairs, parking signage, listed‑building consent for the viaduct—because those are things the council, landowners and statutory consultees can change. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

The Fairies’ Chapel and the Healey Dwarf belong to a different archive: folklore. Nineteenth‑century writers and local collectors, notably the county antiquarian tradition and later local compilers, set down tales about a natural recess in the rock that looked a little like an altar and could be called a chapel. Early print references—quoted in modern guides—describe a hidden pulpit‑like formation revealed when a flood washed away a covering ledge; later colourful retellings add a Fairy Queen, a Fairy King and a bewitched dwarf or witch‑figure, motifs common to British fairy lore. Those stories come from literary and folkloric sources rather than parish registers, court records or archaeological excavation reports; they are valuable for what they tell us about local imagination and nineteenth‑century reading habits, not as evidence of the supernatural. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

You can still see the place‑name on the ground. Local walking leaflets and heritage trails mark a route down to the feature and signposts to a ‘Fairy Chapel’ appear on nearby footpaths and at the steps off Station Road. Community events and the Tearooms’ heritage material reproduce the old legends for visitors, which keeps the stories alive. None of these modern references change the distinction: a name, an attractive rock formation and repeated storytelling are not proof of otherworldly residents. ([whitworth.gov.uk](https://www.whitworth.gov.uk/uploads/walkingdocuments/files/WALK%206%20Healey%20Dell%20-%20captioned%20viaduct.pdf))

What remains uncertain—and worth noting—is provenance. Some of the best‑known versions of the Healey tales were shaped by nineteenth‑century collectors and local storytellers; when folklore circulates in print, oral tradition and tourism literature it can harden into ‘local history’ in popular memory. Where claims involve specific historical persons, dates or events, they should be tested against archival material; in the case of the Fairies’ Chapel, the archive records the place and the stories about it, not supernatural events. If you want proof, visit the council‑maintained reserve, look up the Historic England listing for the viaduct and read the nineteenth‑century sources for yourself—then decide whether the place’s atmosphere does the rest. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

articles.title: Rochdale Council Rejects Takeaway Application on Health Grounds
articles.excerpt: Plans for a new takeaway at 159 Yorkshire Street in Rochdale have been rejected by the council due to concerns over public health and the existing number of fast-food outlets in the area.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has refused an application for a new takeaway at 159 Yorkshire Street, citing health concerns related to the high number of existing fast-food establishments in the area. The proposal, submitted by Sheeraz Ahmed, aimed to convert the former Ria Money Transfer shop into a takeaway primarily focused on collection and delivery.

The application detailed plans for a business serving a variety of hot food products, including burgers, fried chicken, pizzas, kebabs, desserts, waffles, and milkshakes. It included internal alterations to create customer serving areas, food preparation spaces, and cooking facilities. The proposed opening hours were set from 11am to 11pm, and the establishment was expected to create four new jobs.

However, the council's planning officer raised concerns regarding the potential impact on local eating habits. The Public Health officer noted that the application would increase the availability of food high in fat, salt, and sugar. Furthermore, it was highlighted that a health impact assessment had not been conducted, leading to the recommendation that the development should not be approved.

This decision reflects ongoing efforts by Rochdale Council to manage the proliferation of fast-food outlets in the town centre, aiming to promote healthier eating habits among residents. The refusal of this application may influence future proposals for similar establishments in the area.

articles.title: Doorman Highlights Normalisation of Racial Abuse After Incident at Ko-Ko Lounge
articles.excerpt: Jawad Ali, a doorman at Ko-Ko Lounge in Rochdale, has raised concerns about the increasing normalisation of racial abuse following a recent incident involving a club-goer.
articles.content_html:
A doorman at Ko-Ko Lounge in Rochdale has raised concerns about the normalisation of racial abuse after witnessing a disturbing incident on Saturday night. Jawad Ali, 20, reported that a woman became aggressive and shouted racial slurs at a black security guard when asked to move away from an exit.

The incident, captured on video and shared widely online, shows the woman making derogatory gestures towards the guard. Ali, who was working for Protective One Security at the time, described the behaviour as "disgusting" and stated that he now expects such incidents during his shifts.

Greater Manchester Police confirmed they have received a report regarding the incident and are currently conducting inquiries. Ali alleged that the woman also directed racial abuse towards him before the video was recorded.

Published: 22 October 2026 Rochdale Town Hall’s Martlet Kitchen has picked up the Trip Advisor Travellers’ Choice Award 2026, placing it among the top-rated restaurants in the world on the popular review site. The award honours businesses which consistently receive great reviews, with their scores placing them in the top 10 per cent of all establishments registered on the popular review site. With millions of businesses from around the globe listed on the site, the award is a huge accolade for the Martlet Kitchen, which recently celebrated its second birthday. It’s not the first time the restaurant, which specialises in traditional, high-quality British food, has been lauded. In his food column for The Guardian, legendary food critic Jay Rayner, described the Martlet Kitchen as a ‘victory of professionalism, good sense and, most of all, great taste and skill’ when he visited shortly after its opening in 2024. The Martlet Kitchen is helmed by multi award winning chef, Darren Parkinson, who trained at Hopwood Hall College before working at acclaimed establishments including Shibden Mill Inn in Halifax and the Fleece Inn in Ripponden, both of which boast 2 AA rosettes. Rooted in the community, its food and drink is sourced from the local area, including Milnrow’s Jacksons Farm, Defiance Distillery at Spotland Mill and Grandpa Greene’s in Oldham. Commenting on the win, Darren said: “This award is great news and we’re aiming for more accolades in the future. It’s about good old fashioned British grub, cooked to perfection, using top quality local ingredients, coupled with excellent service.” Restaurant Manager, Sarah Crabtree, said: “I’m so proud of what we’ve achieved. I think one of the keys to the Martlet’s success is that we change the menu regularly to keep it fresh and seasonal, but we also keep the old favourites that people particularly enjoy, like fish and chips. Everyone who works here takes huge pride in their job, so the experience for the customers is really consistent. You know you will get excellent service and food every time you come in.” As well as breakfast and lunch, the Martlet Kitchen offers a fine dining experience on Saturday nights and a Friday grill club. The venue’s unique setting in the Grade I-listed Rochdale Town Hall has also enabled it to offer unique experiences, with a recently launched private dining offer giving guests the chance to dine in the Mayor’s reception room. Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and culture, said: “When we spearheaded the restoration of the town hall, with the support for the National Lottery Heritage Fund, we wanted every part of its operation to live up to this building’s grandeur and The Martlet Kitchen has delivered this in spades. To have our visitors place it among the top restaurants in operation is incredibly special and long may people enjoy this wonderful place.” Related content Councillor Sue Smith Council news from across the borough of Rochdale The Martlet Kitchen Was this page helpful? articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council Invites Feedback on Proposed Customer Access Strategy
articles.excerpt: Residents are encouraged to share their views on the proposed Customer Access & Experience Strategy, which aims to enhance how the public interacts with the Council over the next five years.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has launched a consultation inviting residents to provide feedback on its proposed Customer Access & Experience Strategy for the next five years. The strategy aims to simplify how residents contact the Council and ensure they receive consistent support, whether online, by phone, or in person.

The Council has identified six priorities for enhancing customer access and nine pledges detailing what residents can expect from the service. The aim is to create a seamless experience for users, allowing them to receive assistance without needing to navigate the Council's organisational structure. The Council emphasises the importance of making it easy for individuals to access the right help, especially during challenging times.

Residents can review the draft strategy and related documents, including the Equality Impact Assessment and Sustainability Impact Assessment, on the Council's consultation hub. The Council is keen to know if the proposed priorities resonate with the community and whether any aspects have been overlooked. The consultation documents are available for review and can be accessed through the Council's website.

The consultation is open now, and residents are encouraged to participate to help shape the final version of the strategy. Feedback can be submitted through the Council's website until the consultation period closes. This initiative represents an opportunity for the community to influence how the Council interacts with its residents over the coming years.

articles.title: Road Closures Announced for Rochdale Bonfire and Firework Display on 4 November 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced temporary road closures for the Bonfire and Firework Display on 4 November 2026, affecting several key routes in the area.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has confirmed that several roads will be temporarily closed on 4 November 2026 due to the Bonfire and Firework Display. The closures are part of safety measures to manage the event effectively and ensure public safety.

The specific roads affected by the closures include those where no waiting or loading will be permitted at any time. Details on the exact roads have not been disclosed, but the council advises that there will be no alternative routes available for vehicles during the event.

Residents and visitors are encouraged to plan their journeys accordingly, as the closures may impact access to local businesses and residences. The council has not provided specific times for the closures, but they are expected to be in effect throughout the duration of the event.

For further information, including a map of the roadworks and any additional restrictions, residents can visit the Rochdale Borough Council website. It is advisable to check for updates closer to the event date.

articles.title: Chris Cheap Appointed Managing Director of Atom Valley’s Northern Gateway Regeneration
articles.excerpt: Chris Cheap has been appointed as the new managing director of the Atom Valley Northern Gateway Mayoral Development Corporation, overseeing significant regeneration projects in Rochdale and surrounding areas.
articles.content_html:
The Atom Valley Northern Gateway Mayoral Development Corporation (MDC) has appointed Chris Cheap as its new managing director. This appointment is part of a broader initiative aimed at revitalising the Atom Valley area, which spans across Bury, Oldham, and Rochdale, focusing on advanced manufacturing, innovation, housing, and infrastructure.

The Northern Gateway is a pivotal component of the Atom Valley Mayoral Development Zone, which aims to drive economic growth and reindustrialisation in the region. Recently, the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC), a 30,000 sq ft facility located within the 25-acre Atom Valley Innovation District at Kingsway Park in Rochdale, was completed, marking an important step in the development.

One of the key projects under the Northern Gateway will enhance highway connections between the site and the M66 and M60 motorways. This improvement is essential for unlocking further phases of development and complements ongoing works to increase capacity at the nearby Simister Island.

Chris Cheap brings nearly 23 years of experience from Avison Young, where he held various leadership roles. His expertise will be crucial as the MDC seeks to implement its ambitious plans for the Northern Gateway, which is expected to play a significant role in the UK government's Northern Growth Strategy.

articles.title: Rochdale and Grimsby Town Share Points in 2-2 Draw at Crown Oil Arena
articles.excerpt: A late equaliser from Ian Henderson secured a point for Rochdale in a thrilling 2-2 draw against Grimsby Town in League Two on October 20, 2026.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC salvaged a point in a dramatic 2-2 draw against Grimsby Town at the Crown Oil Arena on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. The match saw veteran striker Ian Henderson come off the bench to score an equaliser in the 88th minute, preventing Grimsby from claiming all three points after they had taken the lead in the second half.

The game began with both teams eager to break their recent poor form. Rochdale took the lead in the 38th minute when Dajaune Brown scored following a well-placed cross from Glenn Middleton. However, Grimsby responded strongly after the break, with Kieran Green equalising in the 57th minute after a saved header from Andy Cook. The visitors then took the lead in the 72nd minute through Jamie Walker, who capitalised on a partially cleared corner.

Despite trailing, Rochdale continued to press for a goal. Their persistence paid off when Henderson, who had been introduced as a substitute, headed in a cross from Charlie Tasker to level the score just before full-time. This late goal marked a significant moment for Rochdale, who had recently suffered a defeat against Crewe Alexandra, ending a five-match unbeaten run.

The draw leaves Rochdale in 13th place in League Two with 15 points, while Grimsby Town, who ended a four-match losing streak, sit just behind in 15th with 14 points. Both teams will look to build on this result in their upcoming fixtures as they aim to improve their standings in the league.

articles.title: Rochdale House Prices Rise to £211,000 in August 2026
articles.excerpt: The average house price in Rochdale increased by 3.3% over the past year, while private rents saw a significant rise of 8.8%, according to the latest figures from the Office for National Statistics.
articles.content_html:
The average house price in Rochdale reached £211,000 in August 2026, reflecting a 3.3% increase from the previous year, according to data released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). This rise is notably higher than the average increase of 2.2% observed across the North West during the same period.

In addition to house prices, private rents in Rochdale also saw a substantial increase, with the average rent climbing to £859 in September 2026. This marks an annual rise of 8.8%, compared to £790 in September 2025, again outpacing the North West's average increase of 5.7%.

For first-time buyers, the average price paid for a home was £191,000 in August 2026, which is a 3.4% increase from the previous year's average of £184,000. Homes purchased with a mortgage had an average price of £215,000, also reflecting a 3.3% rise from £208,000 in August 2025.

These figures indicate a continuing trend of rising housing costs in Rochdale, which may impact affordability for local residents. The ONS advises that local housing data can be more variable due to the smaller number of properties involved, and they recommend looking at trends over a longer period for a clearer picture.

articles.title: East Lancashire Railway steam gala draws more than 2,000 passengers as numbers rise 21.4 per cent
articles.excerpt: Four visiting engines, late trains and a tribute to preservation pioneer Richard Greenwood marked a busy autumn gala on the heritage railway serving Heywood.
articles.content_html:
More than 2,000 passengers visited East Lancashire Railway's Autumn Steam Gala as four visiting locomotives helped deliver a 21.4 per cent increase in passenger numbers on last year's event, according to the railway.

The heritage line, which serves Heywood, held the gala from 16 to 18 October. Three of the four visiting engines were making their first appearances on the ELR, with autumn colours along the Irwell Valley providing the backdrop to a packed weekend of passenger trains, goods workings and late evening journeys.

A first visit from the Bluebell Railway

One of the headline visitors was South Eastern & Chatham Railway Class O1 No. 65, which travelled from the Bluebell Railway for what the ELR described as its furthest ever visit north.

Built at Ashford in 1896 and rebuilt into its present form in 1908, No. 65 appeared in ornate green SECR Wainwright goods livery. It joined resident Lancashire & Yorkshire engines 1300 and 752 in marking significant anniversaries connected with 1896.

Both resident engines received fresh paintwork in lined Lancashire & Yorkshire livery for the gala. No. 1300's finishing touches were completed the day before the event by the railway's resident Heritage Painters team.

Last chance to ride behind visiting pannier tank

Great Western pannier tank No. 7714 arrived from the Severn Valley Railway, courtesy of the SVR Pannier Tank Fund. Built in Stoke-on-Trent by Kerr, Stuart & Co. in 1930, the engine faced south during the gala, giving photographers a different view of the line.

Photographic run pasts with the railway's goods train at Burrs Country Park raised £493 in cash donations. The ELR says passengers have a final opportunity to travel behind No. 7714 on 24 and 25 October before it returns to the West Midlands.

LSWR S15 No. 30506, owned by the Urie Locomotive Society and visiting from the Mid Hants Railway, returned to the ELR for the first time since the 1993 Festival of Steam. It is due to haul scheduled steam services on 31 October and 1 November, as well as taking part in a photographic charter.

The fourth visitor, Hudswell Clarke No. 1208, also made its ELR debut. Usually based at the Embsay & Bolton Abbey Railway and owned by Stephen Middleton, the industrial tank engine worked shuttles to Ramsbottom and paired with No. 65. It carried names from different stages of its working life, including Harold, Illingworth and Mitchell.

Remembering a preservation pioneer

Resident engines City of Wells, Standard 4MT No. 80097 and Lancashire & Yorkshire Pug No. 11243 also featured during the weekend.

Friday included a tribute to preservation pioneer Richard Greenwood, who died earlier this year. Engines 752 and City of Wells, both associated with his preservation work, ran together while his family and friends travelled in the Lancashire & Yorkshire Directors Saloon. The railway said his ashes were scattered into the firebox as the train departed.

Saturday's programme continued after dark, with brake van journeys behind visiting Southern engines, a rare trip into Rawtenstall's bay platform and late passenger workings.

More than 250 volunteer turns

The ELR said more than 250 volunteer turns were needed to deliver the weekend.

General manager Lee Kenny said: “These are results that everyone involved can take pride in. They reflect a great deal of work before the first train runs, throughout the weekend and after the last visitors have gone home.”

He thanked the crews, station teams, stewards, cleaners, catering staff and those responsible for preparing and maintaining the railway, alongside the small team organising the event.

“The gala depends on people across the railway working together, and we are very grateful for the effort and commitment that went into this year's event,” he said.

The railway said the passenger increase helped raise funds for ongoing preservation. Transport for No. 65 was supported by the East Lancashire Railway Preservation Society and a private individual.

What is coming next?

The Lancashire & Yorkshire Running Day on 14 November is due to feature engines 752 and 1300 together on the steam service. Pug No. 11243 is also expected to offer short driver experiences around Bury Bolton Street station limits for a small fee. The Directors Saloon is due to offer another opportunity to travel.

The ELR has also announced provisional enthusiast event dates for 2027, when it will mark 40 years since reopening between Bury and Ramsbottom:

6 February: Winter Warmer Diesel Running Day.

19 February: Roch Valley L&Y Pug Railtour Anniversary, with brake van specials planned to mark 60 years since the final Whitworth branch railtours.

20 February: Lancashire & Yorkshire Running Day.

12 to 14 March: Spring Steam Gala.

10 April: Lancashire & Yorkshire Running Day.

1 to 4 July: Summer Diesel Gala.

23 to 25 July: 40th Anniversary of the ELR Gala.

11 September: L&YR Running Day.

24 to 26 September: Autumn Diesel Gala.

15 to 17 October: Autumn Steam Gala.

6 November: L&YR Running Day.

These dates and locomotive appearances are provisional. Check the railway's latest information before travelling at https://www.eastlancsrailway.org.uk.

Anyone interested in volunteering can find details of departments and recruitment tours at https://www.elrps.co.uk/volunteering.
